# Syringomyelia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Neurosurgery > Syringomyelia*

[Original Article Link](/library/OR0IMf)

---

## Summary

Syringomyelia is a condition in which an abnormal fluid-filled cavity, or syrinx, develops within the <u>central canal</u> of the spinal cord. The syrinx is a result of disrupted <u>CSF</u> drainage from the <u>central canal</u>, commonly caused by a <u>Chiari malformation</u> or previous trauma to the cervical or <u>thoracic spine</u>. In select cases, the syrinx may occur in the <u>brainstem</u>, and is then referred to as <u>syringobulbia</u>. The syrinx initially compresses and permanently damages crossing fibers of the <u>spinothalamic tract</u>. Further expansion may affect other tracts of the spinal cord. Symptoms include <u>dissociated sensory loss</u>, presenting as a cape-like distribution of decreased <u>sensitivity</u> to <u>pain</u> and temperature, and flaccid <u>atrophic</u> <u>paralysis</u> in the upper extremities. <u>MRI</u> is the diagnostic modality of choice. Treatment depends on clinical features and associated findings. Symptomatic treatment commonly suffices in stable courses of disease, while patients with progressive neurological deterioration require surgical decompression.

---

## Etiology

* Arnold-<u>chiari malformation</u>, especially type I (most common cause)  [[1]](/library/d-aowM)

* Posttraumatic SCI (3–4% of patients with SCI develop symptomatic syringomyelia)

* Postinflammatory: <u>transverse myelitis</u>, arachnoiditis

* Postinfectious (<u>meningitis</u>)

* Intramedullar tumors: <u>ependymoma</u>, <u>hemangioblastoma</u>

* <u>Scoliosis</u>

* Other congenital <u>malformations</u>: <u>tethered spinal cord syndrome</u>

* <u>Idiopathic</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

* Obstructed <u>central canal</u> of spinal cord (usually in the <u>cervical spine</u>, the thoracic or <u>lumbar spine</u> are less commonly affected);   → impaired <u>CSF</u> drainage → formation of a dilated fluid-filled cavity in central spinal cord (syrinx) → compression of the <u>anterior</u> white commissure and damage (with <u>reactive gliosis</u>) to crossing neural fibers (from the second-order <u>neurons</u>) of the <u>lateral</u> <u>spinothalamic tract</u> first (which affect <u>pain</u> and temperature) → bilateral <u>dissociated sensory loss</u> and <u>dysesthetic pain</u>

* Expansion of the syrinx may damage: [[2]](/library/JaaslQ)

* <u>Lower motor neurons</u> in the <u>anterior horns</u> at segment level → initially bilateral <u>weakness</u> → eventual bilateral <u>flaccid paresis</u> and muscle <u>atrophy</u>

* <u>Upper motor neurons</u> in the <u>medial</u> part of the <u>lateral corticospinal tract</u> → unilateral or bilateral <u>spastic paresis</u> below the level of the syrinx

* Descending <u>hypothalamic</u> fibers in T1 to T4 cord segments → <u>Horner syndrome</u>

* <u>Posterior column</u> (advanced disease) → loss of position sense and <u>vibration sense</u> in the feet [[3]](/library/paaLlQ)

* Medulla → <u>syringobulbia</u>

* Hydromyelia: an abnormal widening of the <u>central canal</u> of the spinal cord in which <u>CSF</u> collects, despite there being a connection to the <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricle</u> of the <u>brain</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Syringomyelia is an abnormal fluid-filled dilation of the <u>central canal</u> of the spinal cord occurring as a result of impaired <u>CSF flow</u>.

---

## Clinical features

* Most lesions occur between C2 and T9.

* Often asymptomatic  and/or slowly progressing (similar to <u>central cord syndrome</u>)

* Cape-like distribution (neck, shoulders, arms)

* <u>Dissociated sensory loss</u>

* Dysesthetic <u>pain</u>

* Muscle <u>atrophy</u>, <u>fasciculations</u>, and areflexia (patients may present with a <u>claw hand deformity</u>)

* <u>Spastic paraparesis</u> of the lower limbs may occur.

* Autonomic disturbances: <u>Horner syndrome</u>, <u>anhidrosis</u>, disturbances in <u>bladder</u> and <u>colon</u> function, <u>erectile dysfunction</u>

* <u>Respiratory insufficiency</u>

* Other: painless <u>ulcers</u> of the hands, <u>Charcot joint</u>s, thoracic <u>scoliosis</u>

* Syringobulbia: a neurological disorder characterized by syringomyelia affecting the <u>brainstem</u>

* <u>Tongue</u> <u>atrophy</u>

* Loss of <u>pain</u> and <u>temperature sensation</u> in <u>trigeminal nerve</u>

* <u>Nystagmus</u>

* <u>Dysphagia</u>

* Palatal and pharyngeal <u>weakness</u>

## Diagnosis

* <u>X-ray</u> or CT: to detect <u>scoliosis</u> and assess the bony <u>spine</u>

* <u>MRI</u> (<u>confirmatory test</u>): detection of the syrinx (may be septated) and adjacent <u>spinal cord lesions</u> (e.g., tumors, adhesions in arachnoiditis)





![Syringomyelia](media/wrfi8e7kiiyn7rcr2r26k23j.jpg)

Syringomyelia

---

## Differential diagnoses

* Cervical disk prolapse

* <u>Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis</u>

* <u>Multiple sclerosis</u>

* Other <u>incomplete spinal cord syndromes</u>

* Hemiparaplegic syndrome (<u>Brown-Séquard syndrome</u>)

* <u>Anterior spinal artery syndrome</u>

* See “<u>Types of incomplete spinal cord syndromes</u>.”





![Brown-Séquard syndrome](media/z3ss1shtbb5jw6rci5u503vk.jpg)

Brown-Séquard syndrome

![Anterior spinal artery syndrome at T8 level](media/uuznwt7vsz3igcvkwmpjk4d9.jpg)

Anterior spinal artery syndrome at T8 level




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

<u>Conservative therapy</u> is usually sufficient, but definitive surgical treatment is recommended for patients with progressive neurological symptoms.




### Surgical treatment




* Removal of the <u>tumor</u> (if present)

* Decompression by drainage of <u>CSF</u> fluid from the cavity

* <u>Cerebral shunt</u> (see “<u>Cerebral shunt</u>” in “<u>Hydrocephalus</u>”)

* <u>Laminectomy</u> and syringotomy

* Suboccipital and cervical decompression

* Neuroendoscopic decompression

* Terminal ventriculoscopy (indicated in patients without <u>Chiari malformation</u>)





### Supportive therapy




* <u>Physiotherapy</u> and <u>psychotherapy</u>

* <u>Spasticity</u>: <u>baclofen</u>, <u>methocarbamol</u>

* <u>Analgesia</u>: <u>amitriptyline</u>, <u>NSAID</u>s, <u>gabapentin</u> (not <u>FDA</u>-approved for use in syringomyelia, but may be considered due to its <u>effectiveness</u> in treating <u>neuropathic pain</u>) [[4]](/library/S70yOh)
